title: The Causal Effect of Environmental Catastrophe on Long-Run Economic Growth: Evidence from 6,700 Cyclones
research_question: Do large-scale environmental catastrophes have a causal effect on long-run economic growth, and if so, do affected economies recover, build back better, or suffer permanent income losses? How important are such catastrophes for shaping cross-country patterns of economic development and for valuing the costs of climate change?
data_description: The authors construct a novel global dataset reconstructing every country's annual exposure to all 6,712 tropical cyclones observed worldwide during 1950–2008, using the IBTrACS database of ground-, ship-, aerial-, and satellite-based meteorological observations combined with a physical wind-field model (LICRICE). Exposure is computed at a 0.1°×0.1° pixel grid and aggregated to country-by-year using area-weighted averages, yielding two key measures: maximum wind speed (m/s) and a power dissipation density (energy) index. These are matched to country-by-year per capita GDP from the Penn World Tables (v7.0) and World Development Indicators (1970–2008), along with disaggregated GDP components (agriculture, industry, services), consumption, investment, imports/exports, government reserves, and international aid. Climatic controls (temperature, precipitation) come from University of Delaware and NCEP reanalysis data. The unit of observation is country-year.
institutional_context: Tropical cyclones (hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones) are rapid-onset storms forming over warm oceans whose timing, path, and intensity are governed by stochastic atmospheric and oceanic conditions, generating plausibly random year-to-year variation in country-level exposure. Roughly 35% of the global population lives in cyclone-exposed regions, and storms regularly destroy capital, infrastructure, and lives across countries spanning all income levels and regions (East Asia, North America, the Caribbean, Oceania, South Asia). Prior literature debated four competing hypotheses about long-run responses to such catastrophes—creative destruction, build-back-better, recovery to trend, and no recovery—but lacked credible global evidence due to reliance on endogenous self-reported damage data (e.g., EM-DAT). The geophysical setting, in which exposure is determined by meteorological conditions independent of economic activity, provides an exogenous shock to physical and human capital that motivates studying its persistent macroeconomic consequences and implications for projected anthropogenic changes in cyclone climatology.
